title: Sole meunière
subtitle: Whole sole fried in foaming butter
excerpt: Whole Dover sole or lemon sole dredged in flour, fried quickly in clarified butter until golden, then finished with a brown butter, lemon, and parsley sauce. One of the great French bistro dishes, ready in 10 minutes.
sourceNotes: Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), meunière method for sole. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), on the qualities of fresh Dover sole and the importance of clarified butter for frying.

glossaryTerms.definition: A French cooking method where fish is lightly dusted in flour, fried in butter, and finished with a beurre noisette (brown butter) sauce. The name means 'in the style of the miller's wife', referring to the flour dusting.
Butter cooked over medium heat until the milk solids turn a deep golden brown (the colour of hazelnuts) and the butter smells nutty and caramelised. Used as a finishing sauce.

content.text: is a whole flatfish, lightly floured and fried in butter until the skin is golden, then finished with
, lemon, and parsley. The French call the method meunière because the flour recalls a miller's trade. The dish takes 10 minutes and is one of the best ways to eat fresh fish.

Dover sole is the classic choice: the flesh is firm and holds its shape well. Lemon sole is softer and more delicate, cooks a minute less, and is considerably cheaper. Both work. Ask the fishmonger to skin the fish on both sides.

items.prepNote: whole fish, skinned on both sides, about 350 g each
seasoned with salt and pepper, spread on a plate
half squeezed, half in wedges to serve

content.text: Pat the fish dry on both sides with kitchen paper. Dredge through the seasoned flour, pressing gently so it adheres, then shake off the excess. Set aside.
Melt 60 g of the butter in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the foam subsides and the butter is starting to colour at the edges, add the fish, presentation side down (the darker side).

Cook for 3 to 4 minutes without moving until deep golden underneath. Flip carefully with a fish slice and cook for another 3 minutes on the second side. The flesh should flake when pressed at the thickest point.
Transfer to warm plates. Pour out any remaining butter from the pan.

Return the clean pan to medium heat. Add the remaining 60 g butter. Let it foam and then colour to a deep golden brown (the colour of hazelnuts). The butter will smell nutty. Remove from heat immediately.
Squeeze in the juice of half the lemon and add the parsley. The butter will foam vigorously. Spoon immediately over the fish. Add a pinch of salt flakes and serve with lemon wedges.

items.symptom: The butter burnt before the fish was cooked through
items.cause: The heat was too high or the pan was too small
items.fix: Use a large enough pan so the fish is not crowded. Regulate the heat so the butter foams without browning until the fish is nearly done.

items.symptom: The flouring stuck unevenly, giving a patchy crust
items.cause: The fish was wet when floured
items.fix: Pat the fish very dry with kitchen paper before dredging. Moisture prevents the flour from adhering cleanly.

items.symptom: The flesh is undercooked at the bone
items.cause: The fish was too thick or the pan was not hot enough when it went in
items.fix: Press the thickest part of the fish: it should feel firm and flake easily. If not, return to the pan briefly on a lower heat.

items.cause: It went past golden to dark brown
items.fix: Watch the butter continuously once it foams. Remove from heat the moment it reaches the colour of hazelnuts.

content.text: Sole meunière is one of the foundation dishes of the French classical kitchen, appearing in Escoffier and in every serious French cookery text since. In practice it is remarkably quick and simple for a dish that reads as impressive. Serve with boiled new potatoes, a green salad, or a few spoonfuls of green beans dressed in olive oil.
